items.title: Bob Broeksmit says tri-merge 'won’t be around for long'
items.description: The Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA) is shifting its push from score providers to the credit bureaus, signaling a potential end to required tri-merge reports . “Credit scores matter, but as we all know, credit reports matter even more,” MBA president and CEO Bob Broeksmit said Monday at the group’s 2026 Annual Convention and Expo in Chicago. Broeksmit has been one of the most visible advocates for a single-pull credit report , at least for lower-risk loans, as lenders face tighter margins and higher compliance costs. Today, most agency loans require a tri-merge report that pulls data and scores from all three major bureaus. Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) Director Bill Pulte recently said on social media that a bi-merge option — requiring reports from two bureaus instead of three — is under consideration, echoing a move that was announced during the Biden administration. He also said the FHFA is studying a single-pull option. Pulte canceled his in-person appearance Monday morning at MBA Annual, where many in the industry expected him to announce the bi-merge option. He is now scheduled to speak virtually on Tuesday. The FHFA recently announced that all lenders can submit loans with Classic FICO or VantageScore 4.0 credit scores. ‘Won’t be around for long’ According to Broeksmit, the FHFA has “known for years that tri-merge is outdated and unnecessary, and they also understand the need to lower costs, fast.” “The specific reform is still being worked out, but at this point, I am increasingly confident that tri-merge won’t be around for long. And the sooner it goes away, the better,” he said. Tri-merge reports have long been the standard for loans sold to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac , giving lenders a three-bureau view of a borrower’s credit but adding meaningful cost to each file. A move to a bi-merge or single-pull model could reduce borrower fees and lender expenses, but it raises questions about data consistency, risk modeling and technology changes to underwriting systems. The potential change is drawing pushback from the credit reporting industry. Dan Smith, president and CEO of the Consumer Data Industry Association (CDIA), said in a statement that “more data, not less, produces better outcomes, and keeps borrowing costs down.” “Lenders and borrowers benefit from the most complete, accurate picture, which is why maintaining the tri-merge credit report is critical to the safety and soundness of the mortgage industry,” Smith said. Other initiatives Broeksmit also addressed appraisal and capital rules, underscoring a full regulatory agenda as originators and servicers navigate a slower market . MBA supports adoption of the new Uniform Appraisal Dataset 3.6 , a requirement that had been scheduled to take effect Nov. 2, Broeksmit said. He thanked regulators for working with the industry on a path that gives more time to prepare. “But as the November deadline approached, it became clear that too many appraisers, appraisal management companies, software vendors — and yes, some lenders — were not ready, and it would be your customers who would pay the price,” he said. On the servicing side, MBA expects a new Basel III proposal by the end of 2026, MBA chairman Owen Lee, CEO of Success Mortgage Partners , said at the convention. “When the rule was re-proposed earlier this year, the worst provisions for mortgages were removed, and MBA has been leading the charge to further rightsize capital requirements for mortgages, MSRs and warehouse. Stay tuned – a final rule is expected by year-end,” Lee said. Lee also announced an “affordability action plan,” a list of 20 “specific and achievable reforms that our nation’s leaders should adopt.” “None of these ideas require new laws. They could happen immediately, with the stroke of a pen,” he said. MBA is also trying to bring more individual producers into the trade group’s orbit. items.title: Credit Score Shake-Up Could Help Millions Buy a Home—but Lenders Say There’s a Hidden Risk
items.description: Real Estate News Follow Us On Google Credit Score Shake-Up Could Help Millions Buy a Home—but Lenders Say There’s a Hidden Risk By Tristan Navera October 12, 2026 Bloomberg via Getty Images The Federal Housing Administration's push to modernize credit scores could change the system, but also brings new risk, analysts say. Financial firms studying the FHA's shift to encourage Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to adopt VantageScore 4.0 expect consequences on the system. With VantageScore 4.0, as well as FICO 10-T, banks can incorporate rental and utility payment history when considering whether to approve someone for a mortgage. In September, FHA Director Bill Pulte said on X that FHA would combine and use the same pricing grid for both VantageScore and FICO. That came after feedback from lenders and consumers, he said. But those changes could insert more risks into the financial system, several analysts told the Wall Street Journal . That's because VantageScore and FICO use different metrics in scoring. If they're used interchangably, consumers could favor their VantageScore, which tends to be higher. Pulte has cast the move as updating how credit scoring works to incorporate modern financial habits. VantageScore believes its scoring might make it easier for 7.7 million Americans to qualify for a mortgage. Many of these people have thinner traditional credit files. "We do not care who wins—we just want them and Vantage to compete—not be a cartel or abusive monopolies," Pulte said in a Sept. 30 post on X. Changing the mortgage game In April, it was announced that government-run mortgage giants Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac said they would accept mortgages underwritten with a credit score model that takes on-time rental payments into account. The National Association of Realtors® and the Mortgage Bankers Association applauded the move as a modernization of credit reporting. And a number of institutions have followed. For example on Tuesday, the Federal Home Loan Bank of Boston announced its 400 member banks could pledge mortgage collateral using VantageScore 4.0 credit scores, effective immediately. It's the seventh Federal Home Loan Bank to do so, affecting 1.5 million customers. Loading... FHA Director Bill Pulte (left) and Housing and Urban Development Secretary Scott Turner announce changes to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to allow them to accept VantageScore 4.0, which takes into account rental and utility payment history. FHFA/HUD Milliman, a firm that provides consulting, data analytics, and technology solutions across several primary sectors, studied 46 million loans from 2013 to 2023. Vantage scores tend to be slightly higher—by annual average, this can be a difference of just 1 to 3 points. On the lower end of credit reports, Vantage had a higher default rate, though Milliman determined both are strong credit-scoring models. Still, the divergence is significant enough to cause pricing differences for about half of the borrowers in the data, Milliman found. "FICO 10-T and VantageScore are two different models and cannot be used interchangeably; both scores require separate approval thresholds and pricing calibration," Milliman said in the report. Borrowers take heed Realtor.com® senior economist Joel Berner says VantageScore requires a shorter credit history and also includes rent and utility payments, so many prospective buyers who don't yet have a solid FICO score can benefit from this alternative. "My take is that expanding credit access to more potential homebuyers is a benefit to a housing market that is struggling for sales volume. Those with thinner credit files, who the VantageScore favors, deserve the chance to be homeowners," Berner says. "However, being forced by the administration to treat the score the exact same as a FICO score seems like it introduces risk, as those less creditworthy buyers can get the same terms as those with comparable scores in the FICO system, which requires more credit history. items.title: Terra Lands $507M Loan For Miami Beach Condo Tower: The South Florida Deal Sheet
items.description: Terra Lands $507M Loan For Miami Beach Condo Tower: The South Florida Deal Sheet October 12, 2026 | 6:30 pm ET Chloe Gallivan, South Florida David Martin's Terra and a trio of partners landed one of the largest construction loans of the year for their planned condo project in Miami Beach. Google Maps The site of the project at 1250 West Ave. in Miami Beach Terra, RG Development Group, GV Development and Lore Development landed a $507M construction loan from Tyko Capital , according to a release. The deal is among the largest to ever hit South Florida, following Related Ross ' $772M construction loan last year for two office towers in West Palm Beach and the $668M construction loan Property Markets Group landed in 2024 for the Waldorf Astoria Hotel Residences Miami. The joint venture is planning a 28-story, 106-unit condominium building at 1250 West Ave. with private wellness and recreational amenities, a spa and a padel court. Plans also include underground parking and ground-floor retail. Terra teamed up with JDS Development , led by Michael Stern , to purchase all of the units of the 61-year-old condo tower on the site for $120M in September 2025, but JDS is no longer involved with the project, a Terra spokesperson confirmed to Bisnow . Northwind Group lent JDS and Terra $98M to finance the buyout. The change-up in the lineup comes as Stern faces a handful of lawsuits over his other Miami projects. Stern's Mercedes-Benz condo project is facing an $80M foreclosure suit , and Fontainebleau Development 's Jeff Soffer is in talks to partner on the project as Stern works on $1B in financing, The Real Deal reported . Stern is also in a back-and-forth with GV Development's Gianluca Vacchi, who joined forces with JDS in 2024 to invest in a $4B development pipeline, including 1250 West Ave. GV Development filed a second lawsuit against the developer in July, claiming that Stern was diverting new investments into other projects and his own projects. PEOPLE JLL hired three office brokers from Avison Young to its Fort Lauderdale office, according to a release. Avison Young's founding partner of Florida operation, Greg Martin, principal Justin Cope and office leasing broker Lisa Blumer landed new roles with JLL to expand its agency leasing and landlord representation team across Broward and Palm Beach counties. Martin and Cope were named senior managing directors, and Blumer was named senior vice president. Martin has 30 years of experience in commercial real estate, with a focus on Class-A and B office leasing, and Cope has been in the South Florida commercial real estate scene for 20 years and specializes in Class-A office leasing and landlord representation. Blumer has more than 10 years of experience and specializes in office agency leasing and landlord advisory. LEASES Terra landed a 40K SF lease with Walmart for a small-format store at Doral Atrium, the latest project in a fast-growing Miami retail construction pipeline . The lease brings the 78K SF development to 95% leased as Walmart joins tenants like PNC Bank, Bonchon Chicken, Sushi Mas, Tremble Pilates and The Good Feet Store. There is roughly 8K SF left available for lease. Doral Atrium shopping center is on the northwest corner of Doral Boulevard and 79th Avenue. Construction on the store begins this fall and is expected to be completed in 2027. *** BridgePrep Academy signed a 56K SF lease at RK Centers’ California Club Shopping Center in Miami, according to a release. A CBRE team of Scott Goldstein and Keith Edelman worked on the deal on behalf of the tenant. The school operator, which has 19 Florida locations, is joining tenants like Planet Fitness, Five Below and Burlington at the shopping center at 750 Ives Dairy Road. items.title: Political Campaigns Have Spent $87M Making Data Centers A TV Villain
items.description: Political Campaigns Have Spent $87M Making Data Centers A TV Villain October 12, 2026 | 3:47 pm ET Dan Rabb, Data Centers Data centers, a once-obscure commercial real estate sector, have suddenly become a fixture of campaign ads blaring into living rooms across the United States. With candidates from both parties attacking their opponents by framing them as supporting the data center industry, the issue could have big implications for who controls Congress and statehouses after November's midterm elections. Bisnow/created with ChatGPT Before this summer, data centers rarely appeared in political advertising anywhere in the U.S., according to advertising analytics firm AdImpact. But by the start of this month, television viewers in 38 states were seeing political ads focusing, at least in part, on data centers. The ads range from high-profile races for governor and the Senate to down-ballot contests for Congress, state legislatures and local offices. Candidates and outside groups spent $86.5M on ads mentioning data centers between July and last week — almost always in a negative context — according to AdImpact data shared with Bisnow . The trend is accelerating: At the end of August, the issue of data centers ranked No. 43 among 73 topics appearing in campaign ads nationwide, according to AdImpact. Now, it is No. 17. The related issues of energy and artificial intelligence are separately ranked No. 5 and No. 20 with $226M and $74M in ads, respectively. The top four topics AdImpact tracked were Donald Trump , character, crime and healthcare. For an industry pursuing an unprecedented wave of development, this sudden prominence as a villain in the national political discourse is raising concerns that extend well beyond Election Day. Data centers are increasingly becoming a vulnerability for politicians in both parties who supported — or continue to support — the sector’s expansion. Industry leaders worry that this could translate into a more difficult regulatory environment after the midterms, particularly as anti-data center rhetoric gains traction with voters beyond the communities most impacted by large-scale digital infrastructure development. “Politicians have identified this issue and are exploiting it to their benefit,” said Adam Waitkunas , president and co-founder of data center PR firm Milldam Public Relations . “They’re seeing all these folks in local communities rise up and make a lot of noise about it. It’s an issue that candidates have been able to grab onto as they try to make a name for themselves in this election. And the polling supports that.” The rise of data centers as a centerpiece of political rhetoric has been on display in Michigan, where backers of both the Republican and Democratic candidates in the governor’s race together spent nearly $4M last month on ads accusing each other of being staunch supporters of the data center industry, according to AdImpact. “They want to take our land, our water, and jack up our electric bills — I'm talking about data centers,” says one ad from Democratic candidate Jocelyn Benson. The 15-second spot accused her opponent, Republican John James, of buying stock in data center companies, supporting tax breaks for the sector and taking campaign contributions from its backers. “He profits, we pay for it,” the ad says. A PAC supporting James responded in kind , running ads claiming that Benson advocated for data center development at the expense of residents and highlighting a controversial data center project connected to her husband’s company. “Residents steamrolled, data center built, and the Bensons could take home millions,” the commercial alleges. Similar dynamics are playing out across the country, with data centers being wielded as a political cudgel by both parties in closely watched races in states like Georgia, Oregon, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. items.title: Social Housing Providers Turn To Bond Markets To Fund Expansions
items.description: Social Housing Providers Turn To Bond Markets To Fund Expansions October 12, 2026 | 6:42 pm ET Sasha Jones, New York City Social housing providers are trying to do more with less as rising expenses and threats of funding cuts butt heads with the nation’s housing crisis. Most public housing authorities and nonprofit developers maintained stable operating margins throughout 2025 and the first half of 2026, but they are expected to take on more debt to fund portfolio growth, according to a new report by S P Global Ratings. Pexels/Whittington S P’s survey of 30 social housing providers found that 86% of respondents expect either no change or a decrease in federal funding next year. About 90% are projecting rising operating costs. Despite anticipated economic challenges, many social housing providers are on a growth mission. Fifty-four percent of survey respondents said they are considering issuing public debt over the next year, with most citing plans to buy or build housing as the primary reason. The majority of providers are in a stable position to do so. S P’s median credit rating for 40 public housing agencies and 11 nonprofit developers is an A+. Unlike in grade school, an A+ isn't the highest score — it indicates “strong capacity to meet financial commitments, but it is more susceptible to adverse economic conditions” than AA or AAA borrowers, according to S P. Since January 2025, S P upgraded four social housing providers and downgraded two. The vast majority of social housing providers have a stable outlook. Two, the Philadelphia Housing Authority and the Housing Authority of Snohomish County in Washington state, are on track for upgrades. Only National Core , a California nonprofit that owns approximately 10,600 units, holds a negative outlook on its A+ credit rating, indicating a chance of a future downgrade. Between January 2025 and August 2026, 24 social housing providers tapped the public markets. Approximately $2.9B of debt was provided across 63 new issuances. The largest activity came from issuers based in California, Texas and Washington, according to the report. Providers have held concerns over proposed cuts and restructurings, but the sector has so far largely benefited from policy changes aimed at increasing housing production. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act expanded the low-income housing tax credit program, which is estimated to finance the construction of 1.2 million additional affordable rental units over the next decade. The 21st Century Road to Housing Act added 100,000 units to the Rental Assistance Demonstration program, which allows public housing agencies to partner with private developers through Section 8 contracts. In August, the Department of Housing and Urban Development updated its guidance for Section 18 , making it easier to reposition aging assets and tap into voucher programs. Still, new headwinds are looming. The House Appropriations Subcommittee on Transportation, Housing and Urban Development, and Related Agencies has proposed reducing spending for tenant-based and project-based rental assistance. Additionally, 69% of survey respondents predicted an increase in administrative burden over the next 12 months, while 48% expect increases in regulatory oversight. Facing pressure, some housing providers have begun tightening their belts. Providers are locking in multiyear contracts, building green to cut utility bills, conserving water through landscaping, implementing technology to reduce labor, and budgeting more conservatively in annual planning. items.title: Receiver Appointed For X Denver Apartment Building Near Coors Field
items.description: Receiver Appointed For X Denver Apartment Building Near Coors Field October 12, 2026 | 6:50 pm ET Cassidy Ritter, Denver Google Maps Apartment building X Denver at 3000 and 3100 Inca St. X Denver, a 455-unit apartment building near Coors Field, has fallen into receivership one month after the building’s lender requested a receiver be appointed to manage the property. In early September , New York-based Mack Real Estate Group asked a court to appoint Trigild IVL LLC as the receiver of X Denver after its developers defaulted on a $170M loan tied to the property at 3000 and 3100 Inca St. Denver District Court Judge Heidi Kutcher approved the request, appointing Trigild as the receiver Friday, the Denver Business Journal reported . Trigild, a national commercial real estate firm specializing in court-appointed receivership and bankruptcy that also serves as the receiver of Republic Plaza , will manage the property. It may sell X Denver if MREG approves, according to the DBJ. X Denver was built in 2021 by Chicago-based The X Co. Its developers obtained a loan from MREG in January 2022. Representatives of X Denver didn’t appear in court Friday and didn’t respond to the complaint by the lender. The representatives have three business days to give Trigild access to the building and necessary documents, including current leases, the DBJ reported, citing the court order. The X Co., which develops coliving spaces, also defaulted on a loan tied to a Phoenix property . Debt on the Phoenix and Denver properties was listed for sale in May 2025. The Chicago developer’s website lists additional properties in Houston, Chicago, California and Florida, with a pipeline of more than $1B in asset value. The company also built a 22-story apartment complex in Denver’s Five Points in 2023. It sold the building a year later to its lender, CIM Group, for about $102M. items.title: Lawsuit claims Compass downplayed regulatory risks ahead of Anywhere acquisition
items.description: Compass is facing a lawsuit filed on behalf of former Anywhere shareholders over the company’s acquisition by Compass. The class action suit was filed last week by shareholder rights law firm Robbins LLP on behalf of former Anywhere investors, who acquired Compass, Inc. common stock in direct exchange for Anywhere securities issued as part of the merger. According to the complaint, the stock offered in connection with the merger falsely claimed that both Compass and Anywhere would “use their respective reasonable best efforts to obtain authorizations and consents… from certain regulatory authorities” regarding the merger. The complaint also alleges that the companies also said that they would do “all things necessary, proper or advisable under applicable law (including any antitrust laws) to consummate and make effective the merger at the earliest practicable date,” and that Compass was in “compliance with applicable laws,” as well as “the absence of governmental investigations and the possession of and compliance with licenses and permits necessary for the conduct of business.” The suit notes that prior to the merger closing, U.S. Senators Elizabeth Warren and Ron Wyden co n tacted the Department of Justice (DOJ) and the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) asking them to examine the proposed merger, claiming that it posed antitrust risks and could harm homebuyers by contributing to higher broker fees and limiting access to property listings. The lawsuit contends that instead of addressing these concerns, Compass instead hired Mike Davis, who the suit describes as a “lawyer, lobbyist and ally of President Trump,” in order to push the merger through without normal antitrust reviews. At the time, there were reports that former assistant attorney general for antitrust Gail Slater wanted to undertake an extended review of the merger to consider any potential anticompetitive impacts. However, reports claimed that Compass and its attorneys appealed to Slater’s superiors including Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche, telling his office that any antitrust concerns could be addressed without a full-scale investigation. In February 2026, after the close of the merger, Senator Warren, along with Rep. Becca Balint (D-Vt.) with 16 other Democrats as co-signers, sent a letter to Attorney General Pam Bondi for details about the DOJ’s antitrust review of the merger between Compass and Anywhere. Investors interested in being the suit’s lead plaintiff have until December 7 to contact Robbins LLP. In an emailed statement, a Compass spokesperson told HousingWire that the “allegations are without merit.” “We will defend against these claims,” the spokesperson added. Related More: Anywhere Compass Compass International Holdings

items.title: Optimal Blue expands into borrower engagement with Usherpa acquisition
items.description: Optimal Blue has acquired customer relationship management platform Usherpa to expand into borrower engagement and lead conversion, the secondary marketing and pricing technology provider announced Monday. Terms of the transaction were not disclosed. Usherpa will be natively integrated into Optimal Blue while continuing to serve loan officers, real estate professionals and mortgage companies nationwide. Lenders typically run product and pricing engines (PPE) and CRM systems separately, which limits personalization, adds manual work and slows response times. “By bringing together pricing intelligence and borrower engagement capabilities, we can ensure originators have the tools to strengthen relationships, uncover more opportunities and compete more effectively in any market environment,” Joe Tyrrell , CEO of Optimal Blue, said in a statement. “This acquisition is an important step towards creating a single originator command center that assists originators to move from lead to loan more efficiently.” Usherpa enables users to stay connected with past customers, prospects, referral sources and business partners through personalized, automated outreach across the homeownership lifecycle. “Eligibility, pricing intelligence and borrower engagement have traditionally lived in separate systems and workflows,” Erin Wester , chief product officer at Optimal Blue, said in a statement. “Bringing these capabilities together and enabling an expanded feedback loop creates opportunities for originators to better understand whom to engage, when to reach them and with which financing options.” Optimal Blue noted it will continue to support an open, partner-driven ecosystem, allowing lenders to use their preferred CRM and third-party technology providers. “While our vision is to provide a single, comprehensive offering for originators, we value the role that our partners play in bringing both key capabilities and choice, which is why we will always maintain an open ecosystem,” Tyrrell said. Fannie Mae direct lock integration Optimal Blue also announced that its direct lock functionality now integrates with Fannie Mae ’s Pricing Execution – Whole Loan (PE – Whole Loan) platform. Through the integration, lock desk users can execute eligible Fannie Mae best-efforts locks within their existing product and pricing workflows by submitting lock requests directly from Optimal Blue’s PPE into Fannie Mae’s system. “Best efforts locking has historically required lenders to leave their pricing workflow, log into a separate portal, and reenter loan data by hand. But mortgage capital markets perform better when lenders and investors can connect directly, move faster and eliminate unnecessary friction,” Wester said. Optimal Blue’s network connects approximately 3,500 lenders with nearly 300 investors. The company’s technology prices and locks more than one-third of mortgages nationwide and supports about 40% of loans hedged and sold into the secondary market .
